newsitem.title: USA: Clinton still ahead as debate squabble flares.
newsitem.headline: Clinton still ahead as debate squabble flares.

text.p: President Bill Clinton campaigned in Pennsylvania and Bob Dole in Missouri on Wednesday as their aides argued over the presidential debates and a Reuters poll showed Clinton in control in two key states.
Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart accused the Dole team of trying to change an agreement over the terms of the debates, the first of which is scheduled for Oct. 6.
"What they're trying to do is renegotiate several points. Our view is we have signed the agreement and we will not reopen it," said Lockhart, who was accompanying Clinton.
"They have had the agreement for 48 hours. They haven't signed it. They are now putting the debates in jeopardy," he added.
But Clinton, campaigning in Philadelphia, told reporters later Wednesday he was certain the debates would take place.
"There'll be debates. I'm sure there will," he said.
Dole spokesman Nelson Warfield said campaign experts were still reviewing the draft agreement before signing it because it contained new elements not agreed to in the negotiations.
The two sides agreed on Saturday to hold two presidential debates, Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and Oct. 16 in San Diego, and one vice presidential debate Oct. 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida.

A new Reuters poll showed Clinton leading Dole by 16 percentage points in Pennsylvania and by 14.6 points in New Jersey. The poll was yet another sign that Clinton remained comfortably positioned to triumph in the Nov. 5 election. Both states have popular Republican governors and swung heavily Republican in the 1994 congressional elections.
The poll came at the end of a week when Dole repeatedly blamed Clinton in speeches and paid advertisements for an increase in the use of illegal drugs by young people.
But a large majority of voters said they disagreed that Clinton was responsible. In both states, only 20 percent said they agreed with Dole's argument, while 70 percent disagreed.
Clinton appeared at a rally near Pittsburgh to promote a new kind of inflation-proof bonds his administration plans to introduce early next year.

"Inflation protection bonds can be a solid rock upon which families build their futures and their dreams," Clinton told a cheering audience at Robert Morris College. "Not a penny of value will ever be lost to anyone who buys them because of inflation."
Dole was in St. Louis, where he predicted a come-from-behind victory "because we have the ideas."

Dole appeared in front of a 20-foot (6-metre) backdrop: "Dole-Kemp, The Dole agenda, keeping more of what you earn." He took off on that theme, contrasting his tax cut plans with that of Clinton, who he said wanted to raise taxes.
Dole said his economic plan "is based on one simple belief -- it's your money, it's your money, it's your money."

Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, who blames Dole and a bipartisan debate commission for shutting him out of the debates, was also due in St. Louis where he planned to continue his campaign to be included in the debates.
